The cross-sectional
design limits the ability to infer causality; longitudinal studies are needed to establish temporal
relationships and examine how changes in grit and physical literacy over time impact well-being.
Additionally, the reliance on self-report measures may introduce social desirability and recall
biases; future research could incorporate objective measures of physical activity and physical
competence, such as accelerometers or fitness tests, to validate self-reported data. The sample
was limited to obese college students from universities in Guangzhou, China, which may affect
the generalizability of the findings; cultural factors may influence perceptions of grit, physical
literacy, and well-being, so replicating the study in different cultural contexts and including
diverse populations would enhance the external validity of the results. Furthermore, while the
study focused on physical literacy as a mediator, other potential mediators or moderators—such
as social support, self-esteem, or mental health literacy—were not examined; exploring these
factors could provide a

fostering both psychological traits like grit and competencies like physical literacy can
significantly enhance well-being in this population. By emphasizing the subdimension of
interaction with the environment, interventions can be tailored to promote active engagement in
physical and social activities, thereby leveraging grit to improve mental health outcomes. This
integrated approach holds promise for addressing the complex challenges faced by obese college
students, ultimately contributing to their academic success and quality of life.

Physical literacy was assessed using the Simplified Chinese Version of the Perceived Physical
Literacy Instrument (PPLI-SC)(R.-S. Ma, Sum, Hu, et al. 2020), which encompasses three
dimensions: (1) Motivation (e.g., “I aspire to know the current sports trend”), (2) Confidence and
Physical Competence (e.g., “I possess adequate fundamental movement skills”), and (3)
Interaction with the Environment (e.g., “I have strong social skills”). Developed based on
Whitehead’s definition of physical literacy, the instrument measures college students’ attitudes
toward physical activity and the extent to which they take responsibility for their
bodies(Whitehead 2010). The Simplified Chinese Version has demonstrated strong reliability
and validity for measuring physical literacy among Chinese university students, with a
Cronbach’s α of 0.86 and confirmatory factor analysis indicating factor loadings ranging from
0.60 to 0.92(R.-S. Ma, Sum, Li, et al. 2020). In this study, the overall Cronbach’s alpha was
0.84.

Well-being was evaluated using the PERMA-Prof

Well-being was evaluated using the PERMA-Profiler(Butler and Kern 2016), a 23-item selfreport measure assessing the five dimensions of the PERMA model: Positive Emotion,
Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment. The translated Chinese version of
the PERMA-Profiler demonstrated excellent cultural adaptability. It exhibited high Cronbach’s
alpha coefficients (α = 0.79–0.88), indicating strong internal consistency, as well as good
divergent validity (r = −0.19 to −0.38) and convergent validity (r = 0.53–0.85). Structural
validity was also satisfactory(Nie et al. 2024). In the current study, the overall Cronbach’s alpha
was 0.89.

Participants were recruited over a six-month period through university health centers, student
associations, and campus-wide email announcements. The study was conducted in accordance
with the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional
Review Board of Jinan University (Approval Number: JNUKY-2023-0154). Interested students
contacted the research team and were scheduled for an initial screening session. During this
session, trained research assistants measured participants’ height and weight to calculate BMI,
confirming eligibility based on the inclusion criteria (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m²). Participants were
informed about the purpose and procedures of the study, their rights to confidentiality, and their
freedom to withdraw at any time

recruitment was randomized across six universities to ensure a diverse sample representative of
obese college students. Measurement bias was minimized by using validated instruments (Grit-S,
PPLI-SC, and PERMA-Profiler) translated and culturally adapted for Chinese populations. To
prevent social desirability bias, all surveys were completed anonymously online. The

The study size was determined based on a priori power analysis to detect a medium effect size (f²
= 0.15) in the mediation model with three predictors, using G*Power 3.1 software. A minimum
of 143 participants was required to achieve 80% power at a 0.05 significance level. To account
for potential dropouts or missing data, the sample size was increased by 50%, resulting in a final
target of 385 participants.

Bivariate Pearson correlation analyses were
conducted to explore the relationships among grit, well-being, and physical literacy dimensions
(Motivation, Confidence and Physical Competence, and Interaction with the Environment).
These correlations provided preliminary insights into the associations between the variables. To
test the mediating effect of physical literacy on the relationship between grit and well-being, the
SPSS PROCESS macro (version 3.5) was employed. Specifically, Model 4 of the PROCESS
macro was utilized to assess the mediation effect. Bootstrapping procedures with 5,000
resamples were applied to generate bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the indirect
effects. An indirect effect was considered statistically significant if the 95% CI did not include
zero. This non-parametric resampling method enhances the robustness of the mediation analysis,
particularly in cases where normality assumptions may not hold. All statistical tests were twotailed, with a significance level set at p < 0.05.

Dear Editors and Reviewers, 

Thank you so much for your valuable comments. We have revised our manuscript according to your comments point-by-point. Our responses to all individual comments are made and listed at below. To find the exact line number, please turn on Show Modification Traces

Response to editor
Thank you for your submission on such an interesting topic. Please address all of the reviewers' comments. Additionally, I suggest incorporating the following key points to further strengthen your study:
Include a discussion on how Chinese cultural factors may impact the constructs of grit, physical literacy, and well-being.
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We have included a new paragraph in the introduction (line 125-134) and discussion (line 417-426) on the impact of social and family expectations and the school environment on students' adherence to the dimensions of exercise and interaction with the environment in collectivist cultures. Also, we introduce reasonable speculation on how cultural differences affect the promotion of well-being in the sub-dimension of ‘interaction with the environment’.

Consider the limitations of self-report measures and suggest incorporating objective measures of physical activity, such as accelerometry, or fitness in future studies.
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We have already provided this suggestions in the manuscript. (line 471-473)

I would also recommend that you use the so called person-first language throughout the paper. Person-first language emphasizes the individual rather than their condition. For example, instead of "obese college students," use "college students with obesity." This approach is more respectful and aligns with current best practices in health communication, as well as contemporary standards in obesity research.
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We have replaced ‘obese college students’ with ‘college students with obesity’ in the whole text, and the corresponding phrases have been fine-tuned grammatically and wording-wise so as to bring them into line with the principle of person-first language. The corresponding phrases have also been fine-tuned grammatically and linguistically to bring them into line with the principle of person-first language.


Response to reviewer 1
Basic reporting
The relationship between PL and grit and well being in college students is interesting, however the rationale for only recruiting students with BMI > 30 is not well articulated in the introduction. This needs to be more clearly justified as to why the entire college population wasn’t studied – I am not convinced about the targeted population by the rationale provided. The average college student adherence to PA guidelines would be very low, independent of obesity status.
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. The first paragraph of the citation adds a description of the literature on the specific psychological and social barriers and higher health risks faced by people with a high BMI, such as research on weight stigma, and highlights the higher need for interventions in this group, as well as the fact that this study wanted to focus on this vulnerable group.(line 75-82)

Clearly multiple authors wrote different sections of the paper without a full coherence check (see your line at 61). A thorough read through is required. Please see some comments below regarding this. There is a fair bit of reaching in certain sections. 
Thank you for your thorough review and for highlighting these coherence issues. We appreciate your careful reading. We acknowledge that different sections were indeed prepared by multiple authors, and we will conduct a detailed review to ensure a consistent voice and coherent structure throughout the paper. 

The references are good, a few more could be added that would bolster the findings of the study. Also a stronger justification for the target population is needed.
Thank you for highlighting these points. We appreciate your feedback on our references and have added further sources that strengthen our study’s findings. We also acknowledge the need for a more robust justification of our target population. In our revision, we have provided clearer rationale, drawing on additional literature to better underscore the relevance and importance of focusing on this specific group.

Introduction
Line 61 – remove “add your introduction here”
Thank you for pointing that out. The placeholder text on line 61 has been removed.

Line 79 - relationship of grit to resilience should also be stated here, that PL and been tied to resilience and overcoming challenges
Thank you for your valuable suggestion. But we have already stated the content. (line 88-90)

Line 135 - remove the word "crucial" as although this is your hope, the experimental design does not allow for the evaluation of "crucial" in this regard
Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We have removed the word “crucial” in line 161.

Line 136 - persistent engagement in physical activity – this is conjecture at this time. Revise.
Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We have removed “persistent engagement in physical activity” in line 163.

Experimental design
Method
It is important to examine the impact of sex on the associations and in the mediation analysis, as many other PL studies and competency studies have shown sex as assigned at birth to be a factor. Sex differences should also be reported in Table 1.
Thank you for pointing this out. We have updated Table 1 to report sex differences, ensuring our results are more comprehensive and aligned with your recommendation.

Also, given the randomizing used why was it that there was a large separation in recruitment numbers of males and females. Please explain.
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We have explained in the Methods section the reasons for the imbalance between males and females in this study and link it to differences in the male-female distribution of obese students in schools or in voluntary student participation. (line 251-258)

How was randomized sampling achieved across universities? You need to explain this very clearly or revise. Line 206
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We've added a separate paragraph in the method to talk more about recruitment and sampling. (line 179-188)

How was the 50% increase in sample size determined? Please provide the rationale for this, especially since this x-sect study was part of an interventional trial (as stated in ethics). Thank you for your valuable recommendation. Our original intention was to expand the theoretical minimum sample size of 143 by 50% to ensure the robustness of the analysis. In practice, we ended up exceeding this recruitment target. Thank you for your reminder; we recognize that our previous wording might have led to ambiguity. We have revised the section on sample size to ensure the statement is clear.

I would like to see the actual normal stats – Shapiro Wilk for all the measures reported along with the skew and kurtosis.
Thank you for your suggestion. Although the ShapiroWilk test is a commonly used method to assess normality, it can become overly sensitive with large sample sizes, detecting trivial deviations from normality that have little practical impact on parametric analyses (Ghasemi & Zahediasl, 2012), So we prefer not to choose this indicator when dealing with larger samples.

Ghasemi A, Zahediasl S. Normality tests for statistical analysis: a guide for non-statisticians. Int J Endocrinol Metab. 2012 Spring;10(2):486-9. doi: 10.5812/ijem.3505. Epub 2012 Apr 20. PMID: 23843808; PMCID: PMC3693611.

Using a Bonferroni style is not needed if the actual P values are reported.
Thank you very much for your thoughtful comment. We acknowledge that reporting exact p-values can be sufficient in many cases and that a Bonferroni correction may not always be strictly necessary. However, in our manuscript we performed multiple correlation analyses simultaneously, and thus opted for a conservative approach to control the overall Type I error rate at 5%. By using the Bonferroni-adjusted threshold (0.05/6 = 0.008), we help readers interpret the statistical significance of these tests in a consistent and transparent manner. Thank you again for your suggestion and for helping us refine our presentation of the results.

I would like to see correlations of the sub-dimensions (line 245) as this is relevant to the study interpretation (you extract single items -like environmental participation perception) and the reader can deal with the issues of multi-collinearity when interpreting.
Thank you for your suggestion.We have indeed included the sub-dimensions, including “interaction with environment,” in Table 2 (No.5). Regarding the description in the text, our intention was not to compare the three sub-dimensions of physical literacy with physical literacy as a whole, because measuring the correlation between something and the larger construct that contains it holds no meaningful significance. We have revised the wording in the text to ensure the intended meaning is accurately conveyed.(line 310-311)

“ability to interact with the environment” is a perception not the actual and throughout the manuscript this needs to be made clear, it would be handy to state the wording of the question in the methodology as you do for other items.
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We have now included the exact wording of the relevant survey question in the Methods section to ensure readers fully understand how this perception was measured. (line 210-215)

This manuscript was ethically approved under the title of “The Effect of Exercise Training on the Physical Literacy and Performance” and as such the current title of the submitted manuscript appears to be a secondary analysis which in my jurisdiction requires additional ethical approval.
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. In the Procedure section, we have added a note indicating that this study is part of the same project survey and is covered under the scope of permit JNUKY-2023-0154. (line 235-237)

The data availability statement is not supported by the consent form nor the ethics documents related to confidentiality (esp since it was anonymous). Please provide the dataset for transparency and replication.
Thank you for reviewing the consent form. We confirm that there is no statement indicating a partial denial of data release. However, in accordance with ethical guidelines and to protect participants’ privacy, we will provide a de-identified dataset upon request for academic purposes. 



Validity of the findings
Line 377 – there is older and recent data showing the relationship of PL to self-esteem and motivation (for instance the play self validation paper by Jeffries in 2021). This also shows the relationship of perceived environmental participation to actual participation which would bolster your findings.
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We have added related references. (line 390-393)

Figure 1 serves very little purpose and can be stated in text in results, and this is not a “model” per se, just a mediation path diagram. Also having it referenced in the introduction is not appropriate (line 137).
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We have removed Figure 1.

Line 357 – the link of grit and resilience should be made more explicitly here. You already cite Jeffries and Jeffries has an excellent paper on how this can be achieved which aligns with your practical implementation statements
Jefferies, Philip. (2020). Physical literacy and resilience: the role of positive challenges [Jefferies, P. (2020). Physical literacy and resilience: the role of positive challenges. Sciences & Bonheur, 5, 11-26.]. 11-26. 10.17605/OSF.IO/SBZYW.
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We have added additional references and provided a more detailed explanation of the mechanism from grit to resilience in order to better support our discussion section. (line 390-393)

And this paragraph on practical implementations makes more sense after the limitations and future directions actually leading into a soften conclusion (as stated below). Also, since this is a college context how and where would these interventions be implemented – at university and if so, by whom or what department, in the community?
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We have moved the practical implication section so that it follows the limitations and future directions, and we have also rewritten the practical implications to better demonstrate how the study’s findings can be applied in the college context. (line 484-499)

Limitations
Limitations are reasonably well stated.
The point about negative psychological traits could stand to be listed in the discussion as a paragraph rather than in limitations and perhaps link this to recent studies by Simonton or by Woolley (which also relates to self-esteem and PL) on positive and negative discrete emotions.
Simonton, K. L., Wallhead, T., & Kern, B. (In press). Relationships between students’ emotional experiences and cognitive and physical achievement during a middle school hybrid Sport Education Tactical Model season. Journal of Teaching Physical Education.
Woolley A, Houser N, Kriellaars D. Investigating the relationship between emotions and physical literacy in a quality physical education context. Appl Physiol Nutr Metab. 2024 Dec 1;49(12):1658-1665. doi: 10.1139/apnm-2024-0082. Epub 2024 Aug 19. PMID: 39159488.
Simonton, K. L., & Layne, T. (2023). Investigating middle school students physical education emotions, emotional antecedents, self-esteem, and intentions for physical activity. Journal of Teaching in Physical Education, 42, 757-766.
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We have removed the segment discussing negative psychological aspects from the limitation section. Instead, we have added a new paragraph in the discussion to address negative emotions, supported by the aforementioned references. (line 428-440)

Conclusions
This conclusion over reaches in using cross-sectional associations and mediation analysis in stating PL has a “pivotal role” line 383. Further, the directionality of the association is also not known, and the authors suggest fostering competencies and grit will enhance well being and this is not a interventional trial, so they need to tone this down and suggest that these findings support examining the relationship through intervention. Finally, the perception of interaction with the environment is not the actual interaction with the environment related to movement experiences, and this needs to be factored in in the conclusion.
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We have revised the conclusion to avoid overstating the role of physical literacy based on cross-sectional associations and mediation analysis. Specifically, we have replaced any definitive language about fostering competencies and grit with a more cautious discussion, emphasizing the need for future intervention studies to clarify directionality and causal pathways. Additionally, we have acknowledged that our measure of “ability to interact with the environment” was based on perception rather than actual interaction, and we have incorporated this distinction into the conclusion. (line 510-522)

Simply put these associations and mediations are important starting points for design of interventional studies as stated in line 124. Mediation and association are the first steps … Indeed the conclusion of the abstract is more fitting with the findings that the over-reaching conclusion of the paper. This difference also reveal an incoherency in the paper, as if multiple authors wrote sections independently and never did a coherency read through (i.e. Line 61 statement).
Thank you for your valuable recommendation. We first have aligned the tone between the abstract and the main text by replacing absolute terms such as “pivotal role” and “crucial” with more cautious expressions like “important,” “promising,” or “may.” In the “Practical Implications” section, we added the phrase “an important starting point” at the beginning to highlight that our study provides a basis for designing interventions rather than a final conclusion. We also made slight adjustments to the language used in our citations, changing “We hypothesize that physical literacy serves as a crucial mediator…” to “potentially important mediator,” thereby avoiding overly absolute statements and maintaining consistency with the overall conclusion. Lastly, in both the abstract and discussion sections, we adopted terms such as “may act as,” “preliminary evidence,” and “Future interventional research is needed” to underscore that these findings are preliminary and require further validation.

<General comments>
I confirmed this study fits well within the aims and scope of the journal. The focus on the mediating role of physical literacy in the relationship between grit and well-being among obese college students addresses a novel and meaningful topic.
This study also confirmed the assumptions of linearity, normality, and sufficient sample size for mediation analysis.
